title: Retrieval and RAG Patterns
tagline: The right chunk is in the index. Will the system find it, rank it first and know when it found nothing?
story: The content is chunked, embedded and indexed, and the question arrives. The system has to turn a few words into the right three passages out of millions. It can miss an exact identifier, bury the best chunk at rank 31, rewrite the question into something else, or answer confidently from a weak shortlist. This world is the choice of retrieval stack and the discipline of debugging it.
oneLiner: Choose how to search, fuse, rerank, rewrite, plan and cite, and know which dial flips each choice.
youWillLearn: Compare lexical, dense, learned sparse and hybrid retrieval and say which query mix favours each
Compute reciprocal rank fusion by hand, tune k and weights, and explain when convex combination wins
Pick a reranker by latency, data path and text length, and set coarse cutoffs and abstention rules
Choose between rewrite, multi-query, HyDE, step-back, decomposition and self-query, and know how each can hurt
Decide when RAPTOR, GraphRAG, LazyGraphRAG or agentic retrieval pays for its cost, with preview status labelled
Choose between RAG, long context and cache-augmented generation, and enforce citations
Debug a bad answer by symptom, stage by stage

flashcards.front: What does reciprocal rank fusion compute for a document?
flashcards.back: The sum over lists of `weight / (k + rank)`, with ranks starting at 1. It uses ranks only, so BM25 and cosine scores never need a shared scale.

flashcards.front: At `k = 60`, what is the highest RRF score a document can reach from two lists?
flashcards.back: Rank 1 in both lists gives 2/61, about 0.0328. RRF scores look tiny, and only their order matters.

flashcards.front: Small `k` or large `k`: which one rewards agreement between lists?
flashcards.back: Large `k` flattens the curve, so a document found by both lists beats one that is first in only one list. Small `k` trusts top ranks.

flashcards.front: What did Bruch et al. (2022) find about RRF versus convex combination (CC)?
flashcards.back: CC of normalised scores beat RRF in and out of domain. RRF was sensitive to its parameters. CC needed only a small labelled set to tune.

flashcards.front: What can the Azure semantic ranker not fix?
flashcards.back: Recall. It reorders at most the top 50 candidates and cannot find new documents, so fix candidate recall before you tune the ranker.

flashcards.front: Why avoid fine thresholds on `@search.rerankerScore` (0 to 4)?
flashcards.back: The score distribution shifts with infrastructure and model updates. Use coarse cutoffs, watch the abstention rate and re-test on a labelled set.

flashcards.front: Which sizing rule links `k` and `maxTextRecallSize` to the semantic ranker?
flashcards.back: Make them sum to at least 50, because the ranker takes the top 50 of BM25 or RRF results. `maxTextRecallSize` is a preview parameter (2026-08-01-preview).

flashcards.front: Why can LLM query rewriting hurt identifier queries?
flashcards.back: A rewrite can drop the exact identifier or product code, and Azure warns about this. Keep the original query as one of the searches you fuse.

flashcards.front: What does HyDE embed, and why does it tolerate false details?
flashcards.back: An LLM-written hypothetical answer. The encoder maps it near real documents, so invented details drop out because retrieval returns only real text. It needs no relevance labels.

flashcards.front: When is query decomposition worth its extra LLM call?
flashcards.back: When one question has several parts or hops. Each sub-query fetches its own evidence in parallel. Skip it for single-fact lookups, where it only adds latency.

flashcards.front: Which question type is GraphRAG built for?
flashcards.back: Global, corpus-wide questions such as main themes. It extracts a graph, clusters it with Leiden and summarises communities, at a high indexing cost.

flashcards.front: What is LazyGraphRAG's headline claim and its caveat?
flashcards.back: Indexing cost equal to vector RAG (0.1% of full GraphRAG) and comparable global-query quality at over 700 times lower query cost. It is a vendor benchmark.

flashcards.front: What does RAPTOR build and what does it cost?
flashcards.back: A tree of recursively clustered and summarised chunks, searched at several abstraction levels. Index build needs LLM calls that grow with corpus size.

flashcards.front: Name the Azure agentic retrieval reasoning efforts.
flashcards.back: `minimal` (no LLM planning), `low` (default, one planning pass), `medium` (adds a classifier and one retry) and `auto` (preview, escalates up to medium).

flashcards.front: Which agentic retrieval API version is stable, and what does it allow?
flashcards.back: `2026-04-01`: `minimal` effort, extractive output and `intents` input. Query planning, answer synthesis, low, medium and auto need `2026-08-01-preview`.

flashcards.front: What happens when a knowledge base is queried without a user identity header?
flashcards.back: Indexed sources return unfiltered results. Pass the user token in `x-ms-query-source-authorization` and set `ingestionPermissionOptions` when you ingest.

flashcards.front: CRAG versus Self-RAG: which needs a fine-tuned model?
flashcards.back: Self-RAG trains one LM to emit reflection tokens. CRAG is plug-and-play: a light evaluator scores retrieval and triggers fallbacks such as web search.

flashcards.front: Anthropic's rule of thumb for skipping RAG?
flashcards.back: A knowledge base under 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages) can go straight into the prompt. It is vendor guidance, and update rate and permissions still decide.

flashcards.front: What is cache-augmented generation (CAG) and where does it break?
flashcards.back: Preload a small, stable corpus and cache its KV state so no retrieval runs per query. It cannot hide documents per user and needs a rebuild on every change.

flashcards.front: Does a citation prove the answer is right?
flashcards.back: No. A citation proves provenance, not entailment. Check that the cited span supports the claim, with quote-first prompting or an entailment check.

glossary.def: A lexical ranking function over an inverted index. It scores term overlap with length normalisation and has no upper score bound.
Nearest-neighbour search over embedding vectors. It matches meaning across different wording and can blur exact tokens.
A trained model assigns weights to vocabulary terms, so an inverted index can still serve the query (SPLADE style).
Query and document are encoded separately into token vectors and compared with a cheap token-level step (ColBERT style). The index is much larger.
Run a keyword query and one or more vector queries in parallel, then fuse the ranked lists into one.
Reciprocal rank fusion. A document scores `1 / (k + rank)` per list, optionally times a weight, and the scores are summed.
Fusion by a weighted sum of normalised scores, with weights that add to 1. It needs comparable scores and a little tuning data.
A model that reads the query and one passage together and outputs a relevance score. It reranks a shortlist because it is too slow for the whole corpus.
Azure AI Search's managed reranker. It rescores the top 50 results and returns `@search.rerankerScore` from 0 to 4.
Hypothetical document embeddings. An LLM writes a fake answer, and the system retrieves real documents near its embedding.
Match small child chunks for precision, then return the larger parent passage for context.
RAG over an LLM-extracted entity graph with hierarchical community summaries, aimed at corpus-wide questions.
A Microsoft Research variant that defers LLM work to query time, so indexing cost matches vector RAG.
A tree of recursively clustered and summarised chunks that lets retrieval pick the abstraction level.
An Azure AI Search pipeline in which an LLM plans subqueries over knowledge sources, runs them in parallel, reranks and merges the results.
The system declines to answer, or says it found nothing, when evidence is missing or weak.
Cache-augmented generation. Preload a small corpus into the context and reuse the cached KV state instead of retrieving per query.

claims.text: Azure AI Search says querying over product codes, highly specialized jargon, dates and people's names performs better with keyword search because it identifies exact matches.

BEIR (18 datasets, 10 systems) found BM25 a reliable out-of-domain baseline, re-ranking and late-interaction models best on zero-shot average at high compute cost, and dense and sparse retrievers cheaper but often weaker out of domain.
ColBERTv2 adds residual compression because late interaction inflates index size by about an order of magnitude.

In Azure AI Search RRF runs whenever two or more queries execute in parallel: a text query plus one vector query is 2 executions, plus one vector query on two fields is 3, and plus two vector queries over five fields is 11.
BM25 @search.score has no upper limit, cosine vector scores run 0.333 to 1.00, and @search.rerankerScore runs 0.00 to 4.00 and is reported separately after RRF.
Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher (SIGIR 2009) fixed k = 60 in a pilot on TREC collections and found the choice was not critical.

In Azure AI Search vectorQueries[].weight multiplies a query's RRF contribution (default 1.0), maxTextRecallSize defaults to 1,000 and is a preview parameter under hybridSearch (2026-08-01-preview), and a hybrid query without paging returns the top 50 of the fused set.

Bruch et al. (2022) found convex combination of lexical and semantic scores beats RRF in and out of domain, RRF is sensitive to its parameters, and convex combination needs only a small set of labelled examples.

The Azure semantic ranker reranks only the top 50 results of BM25 or RRF, cannot rerun the query to find new documents, takes up to 2,000 tokens per document into summarisation and passes a summary string capped at 2,048 tokens.
Adding an orderBy clause when applying semantic ranking returns HTTP 400, and an empty search string or search=* cannot be semantically ranked.
With the semantic ranker on 2024-05-01-preview or later, set k and maxTextRecallSize to sum to at least 50, then restrict results with top.
The distribution of @search.rerankerScore varies with infrastructure conditions and ranking model updates, so minimum thresholds should not be too granular.
Cohere rerank-v4.0 models take 32k tokens of context and rerank-v3.5 takes 4096 tokens, and Cohere recommends YAML strings for structured documents.
CRAG uses a lightweight retrieval evaluator to score document quality and trigger actions such as web search, and filters with decompose-then-recompose.
Self-RAG trains one language model with reflection tokens to decide when to retrieve and to critique passages and its own output, and the paper reports 7B and 13B models.

Azure queryRewrites accepts generative|count-N with N from 1 to 10, requires queryLanguage and semantic ranking, is a preview feature, and the docs warn rewrites may drop exact identifiers or product codes.
Anthropic reports contextual embeddings cut top-20 retrieval failures by 35% (5.7% to 3.7%), adding contextual BM25 gives 49% (to 2.9%) and adding reranking gives 67%.

Azure query hints are best effort, are not applied at minimal effort, and at other efforts a GPT-4o or GPT-4.1 family planner returns HTTP 400 if stored hints contain a filter (preview, 2026-08-01-preview).

Agentic retrieval reasoning efforts are minimal (no LLM planning), low (default, one planning pass, 5,000 answer tokens), medium (semantic classifier and one retry, 10,000 answer tokens) and auto (needs 2026-08-01-preview and a model on the knowledge base).

The stable 2026-04-01 API for agentic retrieval supports minimal effort with intents input and extractive output. Query planning, answer synthesis, low, medium, auto, messages input and SSE streaming need 2026-08-01-preview.

For indexed knowledge sources, the user token (scope https://search.azure.com/.default) goes in x-ms-query-source-authorization. If the identity is omitted, or ingestionPermissionOptions was not set at creation, results are unfiltered.
Agentic retrieval maxRuntimeInSeconds has a minimum of 10, a default of 90 and a maximum of 600, and a knowledge base holds up to 10 knowledge sources on most paid tiers and 3 on Free.

LazyGraphRAG (Microsoft Research blog, 2024-11-25) reports indexing cost identical to vector RAG and 0.1% of full GraphRAG, and comparable answer quality to GraphRAG global search at more than 700 times lower query cost. An editor's note of 2025-06-06 says it reached Microsoft Discovery and Azure Local in public preview.
RAPTOR paired with GPT-4 improved the best QuALITY result by 20% (absolute).
Azure OpenAI On Your Data retires 2026-10-14, and Microsoft recommends Foundry Agent Service with Foundry IQ.

The agentic retrieval planner model list (page updated 2026-09-17) includes gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, gpt-5-nano, gpt-5.1, gpt-5.2, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5.4-nano, and marks the GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 families deprecated.

Li et al. (2024) found long-context models beat RAG on average when resourced enough, but RAG is much cheaper, and their Self-Route sends each query to RAG or long context based on model self-reflection.
In NoLiMa, 11 of 13 models fell below 50% of their short-context baseline at 32K tokens, and GPT-4o dropped from 99.3% to 69.7%.

Anthropic Citations: enabling citations with structured outputs returns HTTP 400, cited_text does not count toward output tokens, and citation types include char_location, page_location and content_block_location.
